title: Small kindnesses
hookLine: a short surah condemns those who refuse even small kindnesses (Quran 107)
tomorrow: why does one verse switch from 'O ye who believe' to 'O mankind'?

lines: A KNOCK: CAN I BORROW A POT?
cards: A knock at the door. The neighbor needs a pot for tonight's dinner, or a bucket, just for an hour. In one short surah of the Quran, that knock is the test.
The surah opens on a man: "Hast thou observed him who belieth religion? That is he who repelleth the orphan, And urgeth not the feeding of the needy." Then it turns to people at prayer.
Woe, it says, to worshippers who are heedless of their prayer, who want to be seen at worship, "Yet refuse small kindnesses!"

teach.b: That last word, al-ma'un, gives the surah its name, and it answers yesterday's question. Small kindnesses, but which ones?

teach.h: IBN MAS'UD: THE BUCKET AND THE POT.
teach.b: Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, one of the Prophet's companions, says in a report in Abu Dawud's collection: in the time of the Messenger, we counted al-ma'un as lending the bucket and the cooking pot. Here's why that's sharp.
The people in the surah are praying. They're seen at worship. What's missing isn't prayer.
It's the pot. The surah ties the two together: worship that won't lend a bucket next door has lost its point. And it doesn't stand alone.
Two days ago, ad-Duha reminded the Prophet that he had been an orphan, and said: the orphan, don't oppress. Here, the very first picture is a man who pushes the orphan away.
So, in this surah, prayer and small help to neighbors belong together, and the small help counts. Not grand charity. The bucket.
And the detail that sticks: in one companion's memory, the word that names this surah meant the things you lend from your kitchen.

how: Surah al-Ma'un is a short surah from the Quran's last part; Muslim teachers use it to show that prayer and care for the orphan, the needy and the neighbor belong together.

o: a large yearly gift of money to the poor
everyday help, like lending a bucket or a pot
a fast kept by worshippers in the holy month

games.q: Surah al-Ma'un, piece by piece: tap the pairs.
p: seen at prayer, heedless of it
lending the bucket and the pot

s: Surah al-Ma'un faults people for not praying
the people in it are praying; they're faulted for refusing small kindnesses.
a companion said al-ma'un meant lending a bucket and a pot
Ibn Mas'ud, in a report in Abu Dawud's collection.
in the Quran, only large gifts count as doing good
a whole surah is named for small kindnesses, like the borrowed pot.

games.q: you keep a quiet practice every morning, and a neighbor knocks to borrow your ladder while you're busy. what's Surah al-Ma'un's point?
o: the practice and the small help go together; the ladder is part of it.
your morning practice already covers your good deeds for the day.
the surah is about money for the poor, not about lending things.
games.why: the surah's worshippers pray and are seen, yet refuse small kindnesses; Ibn Mas'ud counted those as lending the bucket and the pot.

practice: Pick up your phone and bring to mind one neighbor, coworker or friend. Send one plain line offering something small you have that they might need: a ride, a charger, a dish, an hour. Keep it light, the size of a borrowed pot.

wordCard.voice: Small kindnesses: al-ma'un, the borrowed bucket and pot that name Surah 107.

orig.note: Arabic: small kindnesses, everyday help; the name of Surah 107.

carryVoice: Here's one to keep: small kindnesses, the size of a borrowed pot. Five of seven from the Quran.
